transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see us today?

I just don’t feel any interest in the community projects and hobbies that used to mean everything to me. My pastor and a close friend noticed I've stopped participating in my usual groups and urged me to seek help. I just feel completely blank inside when I try to do the things I used to love.

Can you tell me if you've experienced any feelings of sadness, hopelessness, or guilt along with this loss of interest in activities, or is it more of a flat, empty feeling without any other strong emotions?

It’s really a mix of both, because while I feel completely blank and empty when I think about my old hobbies, underneath there is this constant, heavy guilt. I keep replaying that awful day and blaming myself, thinking that if I had just moved the group faster or waited for the next light, those teenagers would be safe and I wouldn't have failed them.
Can you tell me more about that awful day you're referring to, what happened and how long ago was it?

It was about two years and three months ago when I was leading an evening historic walking tour in downtown Belvidere, and a speeding pickup truck ran a red light at a crosswalk. It struck a group of teenagers, killing one boy and badly injuring another girl I knew from our community garden. I wasn't physically hurt, but I stayed with them in the chaos trying to comfort them, and I had to keep replaying that awful scene for the police and reporters afterward.
Did you experience any intense fear, helplessness, or horror during or immediately after the accident, or was your primary emotional response guilt and self-blame from the beginning?

During the accident itself, it was absolute horror, panic, and chaos as I tried to comfort those injured kids in the street. But almost immediately afterward, the intense guilt and self-blame took over, and thinking I should have walked faster or waited for the next light has become the heaviest, most persistent feeling I carry.

Have you experienced any periods of time since the accident where your feelings of guilt and self-blame have decreased or seemed more manageable, or have they remained relatively constant over the past two years?

No, they haven't gotten any better; they have remained constant and heavy over the last two years. It feels like a persistent dark cloud that just won't lift, and I constantly struggle with the feeling that I failed those kids, no matter what anyone else tells me.

Can you describe if there are any specific triggers, such as anniversaries of the accident, news reports, or encounters with reminders of the event, that make your feelings of guilt, blankness, or horror worsen, or if these feelings are consistently present regardless of the situation?

While that heavy guilt is always there in the background, certain triggers make things much worse. Hearing screeching tires or seeing a truck at a crosswalk puts me right back on that corner, making me feel sick and shaky. Even hearing someone talk about car accidents or my old tour route makes my chest tighten, so I go completely out of my way to avoid that intersection.

Can you tell me more about how you avoid that intersection and other reminders of the accident, and if these avoidance behaviors help reduce your feelings of guilt and anxiety, or do they seem to have little effect on your overall emotional state?

I take the long way around town to completely avoid that intersection, and I immediately shut down or change the subject if anyone mentions car accidents because my chest starts to tighten. While avoiding these things stops me from panicking in the moment, it doesn't help my overall state; I still carry that heavy, constant mix of guilt and dread every single day.
Do you experience vivid, intrusive memories or flashbacks of the accident, where you feel like you're reliving the event, in addition to the guilt and emotional numbness you've described?

Yes, I absolutely do. Out of nowhere, especially if I hear tires screech or see a truck at a crosswalk, I'm suddenly right back on that corner hearing the thud and the screaming all over again. It feels so incredibly vivid that it leaves me feeling completely sick and shaky, even though I know I'm actually safe on the sidewalk.
During these flashbacks, do you feel like you're observing yourself from outside your body or detached from the experience, as if it's happening to someone else?

No, I don't feel like I'm outside my body or detached at all. In fact, it's the exact opposite—I feel very much in my body and the experience is terrifyingly real, like I am right back on that corner in that exact moment.
Have you ever felt like you were in a daze or detached from the world around you after the accident, as if things weren't real, or has that not been part of your experience?

No, I haven't really experienced feeling like things around me aren't real or being in that kind of a daze. However, I do feel very disconnected from other people, almost like I'm behind a pane of glass watching everyone else live their lives.

You mentioned feeling disconnected from others like you're behind a pane of glass, but can you tell me if you've also felt disconnected from yourself or your emotions at any point since the accident, or is this feeling more about being disconnected from other people and the world around you?

The feeling of being behind a pane of glass is really about feeling disconnected from other people, like I'm watching their warmth and conversations but just can't join in. I don't feel detached from my physical self, but I do feel emotionally empty or "blank" inside. That emptiness makes it very hard to feel genuine happiness or relate to anyone the way I used to.

Do you ever have moments or days where you feel a slight return of your previous emotional responsiveness or interest in activities, even if it's fleeting, or has your emotional state remained consistently flat and unresponsive since the accident?

No, my emotional state has been consistently flat and unresponsive ever since the accident. I just feel completely blank inside, and this heavy cloud of guilt and dread makes it impossible to remember what it feels like to be genuinely happy or interested in anything, even for a fleeting moment.
